name: Fatima Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time for this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a lineworker in the Northfield district, which is farming country, so it's long rural lines, irrigation pumps, grain dryers, and a lot of driving between them. In harvest season the farmers run everything at once and the old lines can't take it, so we're out replacing transformers and fixing faults at all hours. I like it because every farm's different and the people are straight with you. What wears me out is the old equipment, some of these lines are older than my parents.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does home life fit around that?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Jonas and I got married last year, and we live in the cottage on his family's grain farm, so our rent's low. His dad's slowly handing the farm over to him and his brother. I use AI tools every day, honestly, for studying, checking specs, even to work out fuel costs for the farm. We've got about four months of savings, and I've been reading about starting my own small line contracting company one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still a good tool, people just oversold it. Like any new machine, you find out what it's really good for. I'd say that to the crew, who all think I'm a bit obsessed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not much changes, and that's okay. I'd still use it every day for the small stuff. My job's safe, our home's secure, so I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep using the tools, keep saving. I'd probably start planning the contracting business a bit more seriously, maybe in three or four years. And keep helping Jonas with the farm books on weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a touch disappointed, but mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI every day. What would you still use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Study, specs, the farm accounts, planning routes on storm days. It's like having an engineer in your pocket who doesn't mind silly questions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the business idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still there. If anything, it's easier when things are stable. Banks are happier to lend when the world's not upside down.

S0.say: I'd say it's still a good tool that people oversold, and like any new machine you find out what it's really good for. I'd tell the crew, who think I'm a bit obsessed.
S0.think: For me not much changes, and that's okay. I'd still use it daily for small things, my job is safe and our home is secure.
S0.do: Keeps working, using AI tools and saving, and starts planning her own line contracting business more seriously for three or four years out. Keeps helping with the farm books on weekends.
S0.quote: It's like having an engineer in your pocket who doesn't mind silly questions.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is an enthusiastic daily AI user with low rent thanks to her husband's family farm. Her ambition is a small line contracting business of her own. She sees stability as good for borrowing, a very practical, market-minded view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and pick things up quickly. Companies will want people who can use the new tools. I'd tell young people to get an apprenticeship and learn the tech alongside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. I'm already comfortable with the tools, and new machines make a small contractor more competitive. It could be the push to start my business sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business plan straight away, and look at buying a used bucket truck and a drone for inspections within the year. I'd learn whatever new tools the utility brings in, and use AI to write bids and manage the books. I'd keep my job until the business had a few contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you see this as good for a small business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a small outfit with good tools can do what used to take a big crew. If one robot and two people can do a pole change, a small company can compete with the big ones. That's how the free market should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guys on your crew think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would think I'm mad. Paul, our crew lead, says I'm always trying to fix things that aren't broken. But a couple of the younger guys would probably want to come work for me.

S1.say: I'd say this is a chance for people who work hard and learn quickly, because companies will want people who can use new tools. I'd tell young people to do an apprenticeship and learn the tech alongside it.
S1.think: Privately I think it's good for me, since I'm already comfortable with the tools and new machines make a small contractor more competitive. It could push me to start my business sooner.
S1.do: Starts a business plan straight away and looks at buying a used bucket truck and an inspection drone within the year. Learns the utility's new tools, uses AI for bids and books, and keeps her job until she has contracts.
S1.quote: If one robot and two people can do a pole change, a small company can compete with the big ones.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima reads steady disruption as a market opening for small firms like the one she wants to start. She'd invest in equipment within the year while keeping her paycheque. Her free-market outlook and adaptability point the same way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be hard, and people should look after their families and communities first. Governments always move too slowly. Better to get moving yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job would go fast. Two years isn't enough to build a business either, and the big companies with robots would get there first. It's a scary one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still try to get in early with robots, maybe become a local operator for the robot line crews, since I know the area and the farmers. I'd cut back spending, keep the savings for the rough patch, and put in more hours on the farm. If we had to, we'd take a small loan to buy a robot or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But I'd rather be moving than sitting still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the farm protect you in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. We have a roof and food, and that's more than most people. But the farm's going to change too, there's robot tractors already. It's not a full shield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd take on debt in a crisis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small one, if it bought equipment that would earn money. Not for living expenses, that's how people get in trouble. Jonas's dad would want to see the numbers first, and he'd be right.

S2.say: I'd say this will be hard and people should look after their families and communities first. Governments always move too slowly, so it's better to get moving yourself.
S2.think: Honestly I think my job would go fast, and two years isn't enough to build a business before big companies with robots get there first. It's a scary one.
S2.do: Tries to become a local operator for robot line crews, using her knowledge of the area and its farmers. Cuts spending, protects savings, works more on the farm and would take a small loan to buy a robot or two if the numbers worked.
S2.feel: Anxious, but she'd rather be moving than sitting still.
S2.quote: We have a roof and food, and that's more than most people.
S2.fieldNote: The farm gives Fatima a real floor, which keeps her anxious rather than alarmed, though she knows farming will change too. Even under pressure she'd borrow only for equipment that earns. Her instinct is family and self-reliance, not government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so people should start now, not wait for someone to help them. Learn something, start something. I'd say it at church and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's an opportunity if I move first. Five years is enough to set up a small contracting firm that uses robots and serves the farms around here. By the time the big companies come, I'd have the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd register the business in the first year and start small, weekend inspection jobs with a drone. I'd do a short course on robot line equipment, and save toward buying a robot when they get cheaper. I'd keep working for the utility until the business could pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit like the start of harvest, busy and hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years do for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'd be chasing jobs. With five I get to build something of my own. It's the difference between being hired and doing the hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Jonas's dad. What would he think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say I'm moving too fast, then he'd help anyway. He's like that. He'd probably want to know if a robot can fix his grain dryer.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to prepare, so people should start now rather than wait for help. Learn something, start something, I'd say at church and at work.
S3.think: I think it's an opportunity if I move first. Five years is enough to set up a robot-using contracting firm for local farms and have customers before the big companies arrive.
S3.do: Registers her business in the first year and starts with weekend drone inspections. Takes a short course on robot line equipment, saves toward a robot and keeps her utility job until the business can pay her.
S3.feel: Mostly calm, busy and hopeful like the start of harvest.
S3.quote: It's the difference between being hired and doing the hiring.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Fatima moves straight into building her own firm, a clear sign of her comfort with risk. Her market logic is local: know the farms before the big companies do. Her father-in-law is the cautious but supportive voice in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses. Learn, save, build something. I'd also say families and churches should help each other through it, not just wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. Ten years is enough to build a solid business and still have kids. I'd be running robots instead of climbing poles, and I'd be fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the utility a few years while building the business on the side. I'd buy equipment gradually, a robot or two as the price comes down, and hire a couple of people. By the time AGI arrives I'd want the business established and the farm work steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: At thirty-seven, what would your life look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small company out of the farm, a few robots, a couple of people, contracts with the utility for the rural lines. Jonas running the farm. Kids, if we're blessed with them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything in this version worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies buy up the market, or that rules get written for them and not for small firms. And that some of the guys I work with get left behind. I'd hire who I could.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses: learn, save and build something. Families and churches should help each other through it rather than waiting for government.
S4.think: Privately I think I'd do well, with time to build a solid business and still have children. I'd be running robots instead of climbing poles and I'd be fine with that.
S4.do: Keeps her utility job for a few years while building the business on the side. Buys a robot or two as prices fall, hires a couple of people and aims to be established before AGI arrives.
S4.quote: I'd be running robots instead of climbing poles, and I'd be fine with that.
S4.fieldNote: A decade gives Fatima the scenario she'd almost welcome: a small robot-run firm on the farm and a family. Her worries are about market concentration and rules favouring big firms, which fits her free-market views. She'd try to hire colleagues who get left behind.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to build anything, and the big companies would get everything first. What would help is fair rules so small local firms can compete, and loans for small businesses to buy equipment. And apprenticeships for the new kinds of work, so young people learn from people who know the land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about rural places. Everyone thinks about cities, but out here the lines are older and the farms depend on them. Whoever fixes them, robot or person, needs to know the land.

headlineQuote: Whoever fixes them, robot or person, needs to know the land.
portrait: Fatima Jensen is a 27-year-old lineworker in the Northfield farming district, keeping old rural lines running through harvest season. She married Jonas last year and lives in a low-rent cottage on his family's grain farm, with about four months of savings. She uses AI every day, leans toward free markets and family self-reliance, and dreams of her own small line contracting firm. She's calm in the milder pictures, anxious when two-year AGI leaves no time to build, and with five or ten years sees a chance to run robots for the local farms instead of climbing poles.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because there'd be no time to build anything and big companies would get everything first.
whatWouldHelp: Fair rules so small local firms can compete, loans for small businesses to buy equipment, and apprenticeships for the new kinds of work.
